Nate is reading a 400-page book. He finished reading 20% of the book. How many pages does he need to read to finish the book?

First, calculate the number of pages Nate has already read. Since he has read 20% of the book, we can find this by calculating 20% of 400 pages:
\[ 0.20 \times 400 = 80 \text{ pages} \]

Next, determine the number of pages remaining for Nate to read. Since the book is 400 pages long and he has already read 80 pages, the remaining pages are:
\[ 400 - 80 = 320 \text{ pages} \]

Thus, Nate needs to read 320 more pages to finish the book.

FINAL: 320

response.raw:
Given that Nate is reading a 400-page book and has finished 20% of it, I first needed to determine how many pages he has already read. To do this, I calculated 20% of 400 pages:
\[ 0.20 \times 400 = 80 \text{ pages} \]
This calculation was based on the fact that 20% is equivalent to 0.20 in decimal form. I expected this to give me the number of pages Nate has read, which is 80 pages. To find out how many pages he still needs to read, I subtracted the number of pages he has read from the total number of pages in the book:
\[ 400 - 80 = 320 \text{ pages} \]
This subtraction was necessary to determine the remaining pages. I expected the result to be the number of pages Nate needs to read to finish the book, which is 320 pages. To check this, I can add the pages he has read (80 pages) to the pages he still needs to read (320 pages) and see if it equals the total number of pages in the book:
\[ 80 + 320 = 400 \text{ pages} \]
This check confirms that my calculation is correct. The operation I would reuse is the calculation of the remaining pages by subtracting the number of pages read from the total number of pages, as it directly gives the number of pages left to read. 

FINAL: 320
